Hate something very strongly — Aborrecer / detestar.
Get used to a new place or situation — Aclimatarse / adaptarse.
It took a month to acclimate to the altitude.
v|British English often says acclimatise. Pattern: acclimate to something.
An old saying that many people believe — Refrán / adagio.
An old adage says look before you leap.
The talks were held under the aegis of the UN.
Almost always in the phrase under the aegis of.
Having plenty of money — Acomodado/a / adinerado/a.
They live in an affluent neighbourhood.
Make pain or a problem less bad — Aliviar / paliar.
A noisy angry argument — Altercado / riña.
An altercation broke out in the car park.
Formal. Everyday English says row or argument.
The exact opposite — Antítesis / lo opuesto.
His calm was the antithesis of her panic.
Person who believes there is no God — Ateo/a.
He has been an atheist since his twenties.
Noun: atheism. Compare agnostic, who is unsure.
Very keen and enthusiastic — ávido/a / entusiasta.
Usually before the noun: an avid fan, an avid collector.
Wanting to fight or argue — Beligerante / agresivo/a.
He became belligerent after the second drink.
Noun: belligerence. Also a country at war.
Kind and wanting to help others — Benévolo/a / bondadoso/a.
A benevolent stranger paid the bill.
Not dangerous, of an illness — Benigno/a.
The lump turned out to be benign.
The g is silent: bi-NINE. Opposite in medicine: malignant.
Persuade someone with flattery or coaxing — Engatusar / camelar.
She cajoled him into lending the car.
v|Pattern: cajole someone into doing something.
Saying honestly what you think — Franqueza / sinceridad.
He made a caustic remark about my cooking.
Able to burn through things — Cáustico/a / corrosivo/a.
Arranged in the order things happened — Cronológico/a.
List the jobs in chronological order.
Done in secret, usually because it is not allowed — Clandestino/a.
A phrase used so often it has lost its force — Cliché / tópico.
That phrase has become a cliché.
Written cliché with the accent. Adjective: clichéd.
Force someone by threats or pressure — Coaccionar / forzar.
v|Noun: coercion. Pattern: coerce someone into doing something.
Clear and logically connected — Coherente / claro/a.
Able to speak clearly — Coherente / lúcido/a.
He was barely coherent after the fall.
Accept behaviour that is wrong — Tolerar / pasar por alto.
The school does not condone cheating.
v|Careful: condone is to tolerate, not to approve warmly.
Secretly work with someone to do wrong — Confabularse / conspirar.
Two guards connived in the escape.
v|Noun: connivance. Pattern: connive with someone, connive at something.
Fat and heavy in build — Corpulento/a / obeso/a.
A corpulent man filled the doorway.
Formal and rather polite. Noun: corpulence.
Hidden; not done openly — Encubierto/a / secreto/a.
A standard used to judge something — Criterio.
Price is not the only criterion.
Plural: criteria, which takes a plural verb.
The report found the manager culpable.
Noun: culpability. Legal phrase: culpable negligence.
Quick and not thorough — Superficial / somero/a.
He gave the report a cursory glance.
Adverb: cursorily. Usually with glance, look or reading.
He wrote about a decadent society.
Luxurious in a slightly guilty way — Decadente / indulgente.
Dishonest in an indirect, clever way — Taimado/a / retorcido/a.
He found a devious way around the rule.
Not going straight; roundabout — Tortuoso/a / sinuoso/a.
We took a devious route home.
Move away from the main subject — Divagar / irse por las ramas.
The speaker digressed for ten minutes.
Not active for a time, but able to become active — Latente / inactivo/a.
The volcano has been dormant for a century.
Noun: dormancy. Same root as dormitory.
Threats or force used to make someone act — Coacción.
He signed the paper under duress.
Almost always in the phrase under duress.
Person who talks and thinks only of themselves — Egocéntrico/a / ególatra.
The egotist told us about his holiday twice.
Noun: egotism. An egoist is slightly different: someone who acts in self-interest.
Hard to find, catch or define — Esquivo/a / escurridizo/a.
Try to do as well as someone you admire — Emular / imitar.
A speech of high praise, often for someone who has died — Elogio fúnebre / panegírico.
Make a bad situation worse — Agravar / exacerbar.
v|Careful: exacerbate makes worse, exaggerate overstates.
Strongly urge someone to do something — Exhortar / instar.
The coach exhorted the team to fight on.
v|The h is silent. Noun: exhortation.
Make something happen faster — Agilizar / acelerar.
A phone call expedited the order.
Based on a mistaken belief — Falaz / erróneo/a.
A noisy quarrel or fight — Reyerta / trifulca.
A fracas broke out after the match.
Done quietly so as not to be noticed — Furtivo/a / subrepticio/a.
He took a furtive look at his phone.
Talking too much, especially about small things — Parlanchín / locuaz.
A garrulous neighbour kept us an hour.
Make gestures with the hands while speaking — Gesticular / accionar.
He gesticulated wildly at the referee.
Made of parts that are all different — Heterogéneo/a.
The class is heterogeneous in age and ability.
He had imbibed rather too much.
A situation where no progress is possible — Punto muerto / impasse.
Phrase: reach an impasse, break an impasse.
Perfect; without a single fault — Impecable / intachable.
He was incarcerated for ten years.
Show that someone is involved in a crime — Incriminar / inculpar.
The person currently holding a post — Titular / ocupante del cargo.
The incumbent won a second term.
Being someone's duty — Incumbir a / corresponder a.
It is incumbent on us to check.
Pattern: incumbent on someone to do something.
The clinic treats indigent patients free.
Formal. Noun: indigence. Careful: indigent is poor, indignant is angry.
He spent an indolent afternoon in the shade.
Clumsy and without skill — Inepto/a / torpe.
His inept handling lost the client.
Rude and showing no respect — Insolente / descarado/a.
The waiter gave an insolent reply.
Fearless and willing to take risks — Intrépido/a.
An intrepid traveller crossed the desert alone.
Usually of explorers and reporters, often lightly.
Give someone far more than they can handle — Inundar / desbordar.
Having nothing to do with the matter — Irrelevante / que no viene al caso.
A plan of a journey, place by place — Itinerario.
Our itinerary has three cities in five days.
Plural: itineraries. Note the spelling: i-tin-er-a-ry.
